description: Somos estudiantes de Uniminuto (Neiva) apasionados por la exploración espacial y la salud humana. Estamos desarrollando una solución innovadora para el desafío "Crear software de monitorización de la salud para astronautas en misiones espaciales".
summary:
SPACE HEALTH is a web application prototype created by Johan Bustos, Gerson Quintero, Juana Flórez, Andrey Alarcón, and Salomón Horta for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 (Neiva, Huila). It continuously and non-invasively monitors the physical and mental health of astronauts on long-duration missions, using cameras and contact surfaces already present in the spacecraft, such as handles. The system identifies the astronaut and generates an analysis of vital signs (heart rate, SpO₂, temperature, glucose, blood pressure, sleep), mental fatigue, stress, bone density, and alerts, shown on a dashboard and stored in a database. The simulator uses Python/Flask, SQLite, JavaScript, and face-api.js; a real environment would use pose estimation, rPPG, Emotion AI, and eye-tracking. The robotic assistant CIMON-SH asks astronauts about their well-being when stress or fatigue is high.

A code audit shows it currently runs only in simulation: the connect button does not call the backend, the chat uses predefined responses, and vital signs are randomly generated, with no physical robot or real sensors. Next steps: connect the interface to the real endpoints, integrate calibrated sensors, label simulated data, and keep human medical review. The prototype demonstrates the feasibility of low-cost, continuous monitoring that detects fatigue, stress, and bone loss early and gives the medical team a preliminary assessment and full telemetry.
details:
SPACE HEALTH: Continuous, non-invasive health monitoring for astronauts on long-duration missions

What it does and how it works. SPACE HEALTH is a web application prototype that monitors the physical and mental health of astronauts without requiring them to wear devices or take part in manual check-ups. It uses hardware already present in a spacecraft: onboard cameras and touch surfaces such as door handles. When an astronaut activates the camera or touches a handle, the system identifies them and automatically generates a full health analysis. It covers vital signs (heart rate, SpO₂, body temperature, blood glucose, blood pressure, sleep), advanced parameters (VO₂ max, calories, PAI), mental fatigue, vocal stress, bone density, and the crew’s overall stress level. Results appear on a visual dashboard with automatic alerts and a confidence level, and are stored in a database. The system also includes CIMON-SH, a robotic assistant concept that checks in on an astronaut’s physical and emotional well-being whenever stress or fatigue rises above a set threshold.

Benefits. Health monitoring in space often depends on periodic evaluations or on devices that need active user interaction, which can delay the detection of problems. SPACE HEALTH offers a continuous, low-cost alternative that detects early signs of fatigue, elevated stress, and bone density loss, all critical risks on long missions. Because it reuses existing equipment, it needs no extra devices and is easy to adopt. The medical team receives a preliminary assessment of each crew member, along with the full telemetry and alert history, so they can make more precise and timely diagnoses.

Expected impact. We expect the project to improve crew safety and well-being by enabling early warnings and real-time improvement plans, while reducing the workload on the onboard medical team. In a real environment, the system would combine crew analytics with state-of-the-art sensing devices and, depending on the vehicle or location, robotic assistants that provide support. Human medical review remains central: the system accompanies, collects information, and escalates alerts, but never diagnoses or clears an astronaut for duty on its own.

Tools and technologies. The working simulator was built with Python 3 and Flask (backend), SQLite (local storage of astronaut profiles and analyses), HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (responsive interface inspired by NASA’s visual identity), and face-api.js for facial recognition. Biometric readings and the touch sensor are simulated in this prototype. For a real deployment, we propose pose estimation (YOLO, MediaPipe) with RGB-D cameras such as Intel RealSense; remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) with standard or thermal cameras (FLIR) for vital signs and stress; and Emotion AI (Affectiva) with eye-tracking (Tobii) for emotion and attention.

Creativity. The project’s novelty lies in turning everyday objects and existing spacecraft infrastructure into passive health sensors. Astronauts are monitored simply by walking past a camera or opening a door, with no extra steps or wearable devices. It also pairs this physiological monitoring with an empathetic robotic assistant for mental health support, which addresses isolation and stress, factors often overlooked in long-duration missions.

Factors our team considered. We prioritized non-invasiveness, low cost, and ease of adoption in a space environment. We were transparent about the prototype’s limits: the current version runs in simulation, with randomly generated vitals, rule-based chat responses, and no physical robot or real sensors. We defined a roadmap to connect the interface to the real backend endpoints, integrate calibrated sensors, clearly label simulated data, and keep human medical review in the loop. We also designed the system so that alerts are escalated to medical professionals rather than acted on autonomously.
